paragraphs.text: To show the just punishment of the people for disobeying the precept concerning the Sabbath, {Jer 17:27} and other of God’s commandments. See Jer 7:1.
paragraphs.anchor: The word which came to Jeremiah.

paragraphs.text: Arise, and go down to the potter’s house.] Whether the prophet was to go actually to the potter’s house, or in vision only, it matters not. This we know, that our Saviour did actually wash his disciples’ feet, and at another time set a child in the midst of them when they were striving about the primacy, expounding to them afterwards what he meant; and so it might well be here. It may not be amiss for us to go down oft with Jeremiah to the potter’s house in our meditations - to consider, I mean, our original, Kεραμος ο ανθρωπος; as the "first man, Adam, was of the earth earthy," so are we ex lute lutei, from the clay, clayish.

Then I went down to the potter’s house.] {a} God’s commands must be obeyed without sciscitation. Jeremiah saw that verbal teaching without signs would not work upon his hearers; he is therefore ready to do anything, or to go any whither, for their eternal good.
So the poet -
paragraphs.anchor: And, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels.

paragraphs.text: “ Amphora coepit
Institui, currente rota, cur urceus exit? ”
- Hor. De Art. Poet.
{a} Officiose paret.
Or, The vessel which he was making miscarried, as clay in the potter’s hand.
paragraphs.anchor: And the vessel which he made of clay was marred.

paragraphs.text: “ Non semper feriet quodcunque minabitur arcus. ”
See Jer 18:1. To the visible word God always addeth the audible; as in the two sacraments.
paragraphs.anchor: Then came the word of the Lord unto me.

paragraphs.text: Make you or mar you at my pleasure: have I not an absolute sovereignty over you, that ye lift up the heel against me, and awake my power by your provocations?
paragraphs.anchor: O house of Israel, cannot I do with you.

paragraphs.text: As the clay is in the potter’s hand.] What, then, hath vain man to vaunt of? or why should any proud Arminian {a} say, Quod potui, miserentis est Dei; quod volui, id meae est potestatis? That I can do good, is of God’s mercy; that I will do it, is merely in mine own power? This man was sure his own potter, and not willing to owe overmuch of himself to God.
{a} Grevinchovius.
As God loveth to forewarn; and he therefore threateneth, that he may not punish, for he would be prevented.
paragraphs.anchor: At what instant I shall speak.

paragraphs.text: If I may see such work among them, as at Nineveh God did. {Jon 3:10} He saw not their sackcloth and their ashes, but their repentance and works - those fruits of their faith.
paragraphs.anchor: Turn from their evil.

paragraphs.text: Not by any change of my will, but by the willing of a change: mutatione Rei non Dei.
paragraphs.anchor: I will repent of the evil.

paragraphs.text: All is done as God the great Induperator commandeth, whether it be for or against a nation, or a particular man only. {Job 34:29}
paragraphs.anchor: And at what instant I shall speak.

paragraphs.text: As he did this kingdom of England; which was therefore anciently called Regnum Dei, kingdom of God, and reckoned among the fortunate islands.
paragraphs.anchor: To build or to plant it.

paragraphs.text: I will take away mine own, and be gone; {Hos 2:9} "curse their blessings," {Mal 2:2} and "destroy them after that I have done them good"; {as Jos 24:20} and all this, whether for the better or for the worse to a nation, God usually doth on the sudden; "At what instant," &c. Mercies, the more unexpected, the more welcome; judgments, the more sudden, the more direful they are.
paragraphs.anchor: Then will I repent of the good.

paragraphs.text: As the potter frameth his vessel on the wheel.
paragraphs.anchor: Behold, I frame evil against you.

paragraphs.text: Currat poenitentia, ne praecurrat sententia. Mitte preces et lachrymas, cordis legatos. Let him run from regret not hasten on by feeling. Send prayers and tears as envoys of the heart. Address yourselves to God, and be at peace; so shall good be done unto you. See Jer 3:12; Jer 7:3.
paragraphs.anchor: Return ye now.

paragraphs.text: {a} See the like desperate return, Jer 2:25; Jer 13:9. Actum est: vel desperatum est: vel expectaratum est - that is, we are at a point, and have made our conclusion. Thou mayest save a labour of further exhorting us; for we are as good as we mean to be, and shall not stir from our resolution. Keep thy breath to cool thy broth, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: And they said, There is no hope.

paragraphs.text: As you forsooth please to count it and call it; though we reckon that we have as good hearts as the purest or proudest of you all.
paragraphs.anchor: We will do every one the imagination of his evil heart.

paragraphs.text: {a} Refert stomachose cantilenam illorum obstinatam.

God himself seemeth here to wonder at the desperate obstinace of this people, as not to be matched again. Like as our Saviour marvelled at the unbelief of the Nazarites, and could do for them no mighty work. {Mar 6:5-6} {See Trapp on "Mar 6:5"} {See Trapp on "Mar 6:6"}
paragraphs.anchor: Therefore thus saith the Lord.

paragraphs.text: A "virgin" she is called, either by an irony, or else because she should have been a pure virgin, sincere in God’s service, but was nothing less. What this horrible thing was, see Jer 18:15 cf. Jer 2:13; Jer 2:32.
paragraphs.anchor: The virgin of Israel hath done a very horrible thing.

paragraphs.text: See Jer 2:13, which may stand for a commentary on this verse. The rocks of Lebanon were still covered with snow: whence also it was called Lebanon - i.e., white. Now the Lord was to the Jews as this snow was to the thirsty traveller, cooling and comforting, and therefore in no wise to be left.
paragraphs.anchor: Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon?

paragraphs.text: Heb., Shall strange, cool, flowing water be forsaken, or fail?
paragraphs.anchor: Or shall the cold flowing waters that come from another place be forsaken?

paragraphs.text: Not forsaken me only. Of all things God cannot abide to be forgotten; this is that very horrible thing, {Jer 18:13} this is filthiness in virgin Israel, which is most abominable.
paragraphs.anchor: Because my people hath forgotten me.

paragraphs.text: Chalked out by the law, and walked in by the patriarchs and prophets; Heb., Paths of antiquity or of eternity. Set a jealous eye upon novelties, and shun untrodden paths, as dangerous. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: From the ancient paths.

paragraphs.text: {a} Vepreta avia.
Not intentionally so; but yet eventually. Idolatry is a land desolating sin.
paragraphs.anchor: To make their land desolate.

paragraphs.text: Whirry and whirl them up and down, as chaff before the force of the enemy.
paragraphs.anchor: I will scatter them.

paragraphs.text: This was woeful, but just upon them for their unworthy dealing in like sort with the Lord. {2Ch 29:6 Jer 2:27; Jer 32:33 Eze 8:16} Every transgression and disobedience hath a just recompense of reward. {Heb 2:2}
paragraphs.anchor: I will skew them the back, and not the face.

paragraphs.text: Words savouring of a most exulcerate spirit against God and his faithful prophet, quem toto coelo hic explodunt, whom they shamefully slight, and desperately oppose, both with their virulent tongues and violent hands. Hence his ensuing complaint, and not without cause.
paragraphs.anchor: Then said they, Come, let us devise devices.

paragraphs.text: As he would persuade us it shall. We shall have priests, sages, and prophets still; better than he is any. Let us therefore stop his mouth, or make him away, there will be no great loss of him.
paragraphs.anchor: For the law shall not perish from the priest, &c.

paragraphs.text: By loading him with slanders, and laying false accusations against him. Some men have very sharp tongues. He that was famous for abuses stripped and whipped, had nothing but his tongue to whip them with. Some render it, Let us smite that tongue of his - that is, tie it up and tamper it, that he reprove us no more. Or if he do, yet
paragraphs.anchor: Come, let us smite him with the tongue.

paragraphs.text: If we cannot rule his tongue, yet let us rule our own ears, and say, Tu linguae, nos aurium domini. And is not this the very language of the Romanists? Non tam ovum ovo simile, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Let us not give heed to any of his words

paragraphs.text: Though they will not, yet do thou, I beseech thee. This is ordinary with good men, when wearied out with the world’s misusages, to turn them to God, and to seek help of him.
paragraphs.anchor: Give heed to me, O Lord.

paragraphs.text: q.d., That is greatest disingenuity and unthankfulness. To render good for evil is divine; good for good is human; evil for evil is brutish; but evil for good devilish. Lo, with such breathing devils had Jeremiah here to do; and, indeed, what good man hath not? See 1Sa 24:17 Psa 35:12; Psa 109:5.
paragraphs.anchor: Shall evil be recompensed for good?

paragraphs.text: He who had prayed so hard for them, could and did pray here as earnestly against them; yet not out of private revenge, but by a prophetic spirit, whereby he foretelleth their calamities auxesi verborum per hypotyposin. This is usual with the psalmist and other prophets.
paragraphs.anchor: Therefore deliver up their children to the famine.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Be killed with death. See Rev 2:23. {See Trapp on "Rev 2:23"}
paragraphs.anchor: And let their men be put to death.

paragraphs.text: The Vulgate rendereth it, Latronem, a thief, or robber - viz., Nebuchadnezzar, that arch-thief, whose monarchy was grande latrociuium, grand thief, and whose regiment, without righteousness, was robbery by authority.
paragraphs.anchor: When thou shalt bring a troop.

paragraphs.text: Though I know it not, yet thou art privy to it, and canst prevent it; for wisdom and might are thine. {Dan 2:20}
paragraphs.anchor: Yet, Lord, thou knowest all their counsel.

paragraphs.text: All malice is bloody.
paragraphs.anchor: To slay me.

paragraphs.text: He knew their sin to be unpardonable; and therefore prayeth for vengeance upon them unavoidable. This was fulfilled upon the Jews by the Babylonians in respect of Jeremiah, and by the Romans in respect of Christ.
paragraphs.anchor: Forgive not their iniquity.

paragraphs.text: A heavy curse. Woe to such as whose debts stand uncrossed in God’s book. Their sins may sleep a long time, like a sleeping debt, not called for of many years; as Saul’s sin in slaying the Gibeonites was not punished till forty years after; as Joab’s killing of Abner slept all David’s days. Men’s consciences also may sleep (in such a case) for a season; but their damnation sleepeth not, nor can their condition be safe till God have wiped out their sins for his own sake, till he have crossed out the black lines of our iniquities with the red lines of his Son’s blood, and taken out of his coffers so much as may fully satisfy, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Neither blot out their sin from thy sight.
